speechtext:
Before we proceed, I
know that the hon. member for Northumberland does not want to use unparliamentary language. According to standing order 41, citation 299, Beauchesne, 2nd edition, no member will be permitted "to impute want of straightforwardness or courage" to another member.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is all right, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member need not withdraw it. I do not want it withdrawn; I want to deal with it.

Income War Tax
If it is against the rules I will use other language.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I Tule that it is against the rules, and unparliamentary.

I willingly withdraw it because it is contrary to the rules of the house; but I am quite satisfied that the Minister of Finance has that abstract commodity that I refer to, and will reply to my challenge on the basis on which I have made it.

I should like to say a word or two in connection with the subject which has just been discussed by the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario, and the hon. member for Fraser Valley. I am not going to demand anything from the minister. I doubt whether if I demanded it I would be successful, in any event, by that method; but I suggest that the minister is far less reasonable than I believe him to be if the logic which has been expressed by the hon. members who discussed this matter this afternoon does not appeal to him.
I tell him that so far as some of us are concerned the situation is completely intolerable. In the first place, I understand it is a principle of taxation that those expenditures shall be exempt which are required in order to earn the income, whether it is a salary or income from a business. The Minister of National Revenue has said, "Oh, no; expenses are not allowed to be deducted in connection with salaries." But this is a very unusual type of salary. It is probably the only type of salary of which it can be said that people have to spend money out of their own pockets in order to earn it. Others who are earning salaries have to pay only their ordinary expenses of living, whereas members of parliament have extraordinary expenditures.
The position of ministers of the crown is not the same as that of private members. Ministers take up their residence in Ottawa; they have only their ordinary living expenses to look after, and probably tie whole of their income should be taxed, since the expenses of their offices, their telegrams, long distance telephone calls, and all that kind of thing, are covered by government allowances. So far as private members are concerned that is not the situation. Personally I keep up a home in the city of Saskatoon, where I have a family and a large house and all the expenses which go with it. In order to earn that $4,000, if you call it "earning it", I have to come to Ottawa and live on a scale which is very high, considering the charges which are made in this city as compared with those in other parts of the country. Members of this com-

mittee know as well as I do that the costs of living down here are out of proportion to those which obtain in most other parts of Canada. Aou pay a very high rate for rooms, fairly high rates for meals, and the longer the session lasts the less money you have as far as your ordinary expenses at home are concerned.
This matter has been taken up at this time, unfortunately, because of the fact that the pinch of taxes has made itself felt in this connection. Actually it is a principle which should always have been operative. Of course as a younger and one of the more recent members I never had an opportunity to take it up, nor do I know whether I would have done so or not. But older members must recognize that in the past they have been derelict in their duty with reference to the position of future members of parliament. In the days when taxation was not high, when it was not necessary to live here for more than about three months, when one could get quarters at reasonable rates for one's family and bring them down if one liked, it was not a matter of very much importance. But at the present time, when in order to earn this indemnity, which is supposed to provide for our out-of-pocket expenses and compensate us for absence from home, we have to pay substantial sums of money out of our income, it is a matter of importance, and I suggest that something be done about it.
I believe it would be a great mistake to propose any increase in the indemnities of hon. members at this time. That would be the worst possible approach to the problem.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Why?

If we did that, every other class of citizen in this country would be demanding similar consideration, because all of them find their burdens very heavy. But there are very few citizens who realize that we are not entitled to deduct for taxation purposes the expenditures we incur in order to earn this indemnity. I have discussed the matter with literally dozens of people in my own constituency, and they were dumbfounded to know that I was not entitled to deduct the cost of telegrams sent to them to tell them something about their own affairs, or the expense of a stenographer when I am at home to take care of the affairs of my constituents, or any part of my living expenses in the city of Ottawa, despite the fact that my family and personal expenses are going on at home just the same.
I do not know why it is necessary that this matter should be taken up in the house. Surely it has been brought before the cabinet

Income War Tax
on previous occasions. From what I have been able to pick up from other hon. members, it has been discussed; surely it should have been settled upon the principle of taxation which I believe has always been applicable in this country, despite the fact that there may be one or two decisions of law which are a little complicated, and probably faulty, and were determined when conditions were not the same as they are now. In any event, whether there is a judicial decision on the subject or whether there is not, I suggest, in view of the arguments which have been advanced publicly this afternoon by hon. members who have done so at the risk of jeopardizing their positions- I say this advisedly-and of being misunderstood outside the house, because unquestionably it is seldom that the full import of a member's remarks ever gets to his constituents, the administration should consider this matter very seriously indeed. I repeat that the situation is intolerable for a number of members who are required to continue to live in the city of Ottawa under the circumstances which exist at the present time.

To revert to the interesting discussion that ensued when the hon. member for Acadia indicated to the minister the state of affairs that exists in connection with the sale of victory bonds, reading a letter and mentioning a certain incident, the committee will recall that he cited a case where a salesman had induced a purchaser to purchase bonds, borrowing the money for six months through an arrangement with the bank that at the end of that time the bank would take the bond off his hands and would become the purchaser. The minister said he deprecated that type of transaction and asked the hon. member for Acadia how it could be cured; whether a gaol term should be provided. With the permission of the hon. member for Acadia I should like to be helpful and to tell the minister how he could avoid it without a gaol term or any harsh or drastic course- and he would avoid it for all time. He can join with those of us who want to amend section 59 of the Bank Act by doing away with the right of private banks to create new money without having cash reserves behind it and, as the minister once put it to the house, to carry on the business of banking by lending seven, eight, nine and ten times more money than the banks have in their cash reserves; because, if that transaction was consummated [DOT]six months later, it was that very practice, described in that last phrase, which the bank carried out when they took the bonds off the hands of the original purchaser.
If the minister really disapproves of the banks acquiring bonds by purchase in that
100-300J
manner, then his course is simple. He can amend section 59 of the act by requiring the banks, so far as their deposit accounts on loans, not including savings accounts, are concerned, to have 100 per cent cash reserve. Let me suggest that it is not merely the transaction that the hon. member for Acadia mentioned that we must consider. There is a much more serious state of affairs in that our Minister of Finance has, in the past two or three years, increased the borrowing for the government of Canada through the chartered banks partly by short-term loans and partly by securities exceeding two years to run, so that now this country is indebted through him to the chartered banks for an amount on which we are paying interest to the extent, on April 30 last, of S2,696 million, or, roughly speaking, $2,700 million, every dollar of which, instead of having interest-bearing securities lying in the vaults of the ten chartered banks for that amount, could have been issued into existence through the use of public credit through the Bank of Canada by amending section 59 as a protection against inflation. If we had done this we would not have been canying an intolerable burden of $40 million every year and down through the years to come in order to finance that type of borrowing.
I commend to the minister this course that I am suggesting. He does not need to gaol anyone. Simply take back for the people of Canada the privilege which they were given under the British North America Act, so that they themselves, the government, shall issue and control the currency and credit of this country which our forefathers gave away to the chartered banks in their charters and which the chartered banks are again to-day seeking to retain in the form of a monopolistic privilege when they ask us to renew their charters without amending section 59 of the act.
That is a simple course to take and I beg the minister to give it full consideration, because if he comes to the banking and commerce committee and says that he believes in using the credit of the country in the terms laid down by his leader, the Liberal Prime Minister, in 1933 and 1935-in terms of public need and not in terms of bankers' greed- this is a remarkable opportunity he has, this tenth year, to come into that committee if he withdraws his opposition to the amendment of section 59. He has not yet declared himself, but I am making a bad guess if he has not yet seen the light to the extent of joining with others in asking that this be done. He will save the country $40 million a year for the next twenty years. He will save much more
Income War Tax

than that, because there is a gap between what we can get by taxation plus the sale of bonds and what is obtained by borrowing. Either he will go and borrow more money next year from the Bank of Canada, issuing it into existence as new money, without an interest-bearing load, or he will go back again with his hat in his hand to the chartered banks and borrow from them at the low rate of interest which he has been able to obtain. Why not issue the money into existence interest free, by using our own credit, instead of appointing the banker as a toll-gate to exact interest from the people of Canada in order to lend money for public need into existence with an interest debt upon it?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We are in committee of ways and means, and I would point out that standing order 58, section 2, reads:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) asked the consent of the Chair and of the committee, which was accorded him, to discuss the question of parliamentary indemnities, but since then some other questions have arisen altogether foreign to the clause which we are supposed to be discussing. I trust the committee will find it possible to confine its remarks to the clause before the Chair.

This discussion on the first resolution under the Income War Tax Act proposes to reduce the provision for accumulated savings, and it has brought on a debate which involves in its wider sense the responsibility of parliament to the taxpayer. I venture to suggest that this debate has already indicated that our Department of Finance has a very limited idea of where it is to-day. It has a vague idea of how it got there, but I do not think it has the foggiest idea of where it is going to land this nation if it continues on its present course. I make that statement because we have arrived at a point where the government is faced with a revolt led by the leader of the official opposition, supported by the two junior parties in the house and, I believe, by a majority of hon. members sitting behind the treasury benches, in regard to the policy of taxation which has gone so far that it has been declared by one government supporter to be a sabotage of the public life of the Dominion of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Nothing like relieving ourselves from taxation.
My hon. friend chirps up with his usual bright remarks, which are just about as foolish as the financial policy he supports.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: About as bright as most of yours.

My hon. friend can continue with interruptions of that kind if he wishes, but it is a very easy matter with which to deal. I do not know of any time in the history of the House of Commons of Canada when a more serious charge was made against any responsible ministry than that made this afternoon by the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario, that the government is sabotaging the public life of Canada. How did we get to that position? We got to it by ignoring the advice of every Minister of Finance who has held that portfolio in this house. From time immemorial we have been advised that it was essential that any sound budget should be balanced out of taxation. Since 1914 we have gone on increasing the public debt, until in financing this war we have carried on, as we did in financing the depression, a deficit system of financing, increasing the burden of debt and taxation until to-day the repayment of our national debt has become a public joke, and we assume that for all time to come generations yet unborn will have to carry on under the slavery of an involuntary load of interestbearing public debt.
Therefore we ask what we must do. Tax the people at the source? I heartily agree with every word uttered by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, that taxation for the needs of war knows no limit; but does anyone think for a moment that we have to tax single people whose earnings are below $100 a month, or a family whose earnings are below $1,800 a year, to finance this war or to meet any other obligation of the country, when we have at our disposal a national institution that can put into circulation the best money the Canadian people ever used as a medium of exchange? Anyone listening to the Minister of Finance yesterday when he explained how easy it would be for us to carry this debt would have thought we were in a comfortable position of security. If the minister is right, then how terribly wrong have been all his predecessors in office. Do not, however, make any mistake about the position he took. He said that the time would come, with a pyramiding national debt, when an intolerable strain would be placed upon the economy of the nation. He did not tell us, because he does not know, when that intolerable strain is going to arise. He did not tell us, because he did not know, what the remedy would be when that intolerable strain

Income War Tax
of an immense debt load became evident. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, and to this parliament that this intolerable strain has already arrived, and that we are financing by following a false course, by putting into circulation a medium of exchange which is merely an appalling discount of the rights and wealth of the people of to-morrow.
We have been told a great deal about the necessity of taking money away from the people in order to avoid inflation. If there was ever any justification for a single word of all those arguments, then the ending of compulsory savings is one of the most unsound things this government has ever done through its Department of Finance. It would have been far better to relieve from taxation those earning less than $100 a month, which would include most of the young men who are accumulating for their to-morrow, and families whose earnings are less than $1,800, at the same time accumulating savings for them to be used by the country during the war and to be made available to the people when the war is over, than to have this provision which I venture to say will meet with the approval of but a very small percentage of even the people who are supposed to benefit under it.
Let me point out something else. When are those accumulated savings to be repaid? How are they to be repaid? What guarantee is there that some government in the future, not the one creating the obligation under a vague and general law but a government forced to carry on and service the enormous debt load created by this government which imposed that provision-what guarantee is there that some new parliament, under the debt-load obligation it will have to carry, will feel itself bound to pay back even the accumulated savings? The people whose money it is have never been given a statement; they .'have never been issued a certificate, or even a book in which to record the savings that have accumulated on their behalf. A great many people throughout the country tell me quite frankly, "Oh, we will never get back those accumulated savings." I venture to say that if they had been given some concrete form of security in exchange for them, very few would not have been glad even now to continue to accumulate. I do not think many people in this country would fear the danger to the finances of the government if that course were taken; in fact, from my discussions with hon. members in all parties in this house I am satisfied that a majority are in favour of such a course. There is one other thing I wish to say: The responsibility is only in the first instance that of the ministry. The-responsibility is on parliament,
and it is for parliament to say whether its overwhelming will shall rule, or whether it shall be the will of one department.
If we endorse, as a great many members have, the statements made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, those made by the leaders of the C.C.F. and Social Credit parties, and by the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario, whose will is going to rule? This issue involves not merely the question of taxation upon lower income earning brackets. The issue raised to-day involves not merely the right of a member of parliament to be indemnified. The charge of sabotaging the public life of Canada could exist only if what the hon. member for Fraser Valley has said was true, namely, that two brilliant young soldiers have found it impossible to carry on as members of parliament in Canada, because of the taxation policy of the present ministry of finance.
Yes, what is involved is the sovereignty of parliament. The time has come when members of this parliament should unite to restore something that has been taken away from them, and that is the right of parliament to have its will carried out by the ministry. The thing that must be changed is the right of the ministry to impose its will upon parliament, whether parliament agrees or not. This goes to the very root of democracy; it is the issue upon which this war is being fought. And that is the issue raised to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member surely has the right to introduce a want of confidence motion at any hour he wishes.

And the hon. member is probably now going to be faced with that issue.
I think the minister has done enough harm in the country already.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not saying I should do anything.

If we are to be told again, " Oh, well, you accept my will, or I will resign," as we have been told, then I shall have to consider what I will have to do about that. I say to the minister that many of us supporting the government he represents have to consider what we are going to do about this matter if it continues.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The only point is this: The hon. member says that this goes to the sovereignty of parliament, and that we must do something to make a change, so that the government cannot do things against the will of parliament. What I say is that the hon. member is quite free, at any time, to take the-will of parliament on a specific issue by moving a want of confidence motion. He is quite-
Income War Tax

free to do it. So that there is nothing wrong with our democratic system or the soverignty of parliament. Parliament is perfectly sovereign. As a matter of fact parliament has already pronounced itself on the issue he is talking about, namely compulsory savings and exemptions.

All right; my hon. friend has the issue put up to him, and he has been invited by the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario, to make his decision upon it. When that decision comes, the issue will be fairly out as to whether or not the generally expressed will of parliament, which, I take it, in this house to-day is something of no uncertain measure, should be accepted. That issue will, I hope, be dealt with.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How many hon. members, before to-day, have risen in their places and said that they wanted their indemnities free from taxation?
They want it; make no mistake about that.

I speak only from the information which comes to me, but I believe that there have been committees appointed, and that on more than one occasion those committees represented all parties in the house -Liberal committee, meeting with committees of the official opposition, and the Social Credit and C.C.F. parties-and have returned to the government, and conveyed a unanimous wish on the part of all parties in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been a difference of opinion among members.
Mr. Chairman-
Mr. Chairman, I asked for the floor in the early part of the debate.
The Chairman said that he would next see the hon. member for York West.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Trinity was in the committee, while the hon. member for York West was not here. I do not say this in any disparaging way, but unless members are here it is difficult for the Chair to arrange the order of debate.

I wish to congratulate the hon. member for York-Sunbury, and to commend the statement he has made respecting the financial position of hon. members. I refer particularly to the quiet, dignified and statesmanlike way in which he presented the subject. While I approve most highly what he said and the manner in which he said it, I also deprecate the violence of speech and the 
extreme statements which have been made, following his address.
On a point of order, will the hon. member elaborate on that statement?

I desire to suggest, also, that I was one of the speakers who followed the hon. member for York-Sunbury. Since the hon. member for Trinity has put his statement in the plural, that he deprecates the lack of dignity of the statements made following that of the hon. member for York-Sunbury, in my judgment he has covered a little too much territory, and I think he had better certify as to whom he means.
Again on the point of order, the hon. member for Trinity has no right to impute anything of that kind.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is no point of order before the Chair.
Let the hon. member for Trinity stay within the confines of the order, then.
I did not refer to lack of dignity on the part of anybody, nor did I mention any hon. member who had preceded me. I spoke about the violence of the language and the extreme statements I had heard.
And I challenge the hon. member to mention who made violent statements; who uttered the violent language?

My hon. friend will put the cap on.
Mr FRASER (Northumberland, Ont.)': He certainly will, but my hon. friend is afraid to say what he was referring to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must ask for order in the committee; otherwise I shall have to use the power I have to restore order. The debate should be confined to the item before the committee.
Let the hon. member for Trinity stay within the item, then.

Because the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario, desires me to do so, I will specify that the statement with regard' to the courage of the Minister of Finance, and the suggestion that his thinking was anaemic, were certainly violent and extreme statements.

He does not need your help.

Income War Tax

Perhaps not, but I am a member of the house, and I am as free to state my opinion on the floor of the house as was the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario. And I say to hon. members that nothing is to be gained in the discussion of our own problems by making overstatements or statements which have at least the appearance of anger. Certainly nothing is to be gained by attempts at driving the administration or offering challenges and that sort of thing. This is a subject which should be approached with the greatest dignity, reserve and care. It is for that reason that I feel a duty to speak and also because I think the hon. member for York-Sunbury has understated rather than overstated the case.
I should like to put upon Hansard some figures with regard to this question of indemnity, but first may I say that I am not grinding any axe of my own. Fortunately I have been able to get by, largely because of an earning power, a very small family and the fact, that, like many others in this house, I have a perfect wife. With that combination I have been able to keep going. I am not speaking on my own behalf; I am speaking because it is the duty of a member to express himself on these matters and particularly to defend democracy which is in danger.
Let me give the figures I have gleaned since this debate started. Let us suppose that a member has no other source of income than his indemnity. If he is a married man without a family he will pay a tax of $1,364 on his $4,000 indemnity. That is to say, he will receive by way of indemnity, not $4,000, but $2,636.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does that include compulsory savings?

It does. I am speaking
of this year's figures and there would be compulsory savings of ten per cent of the gross income. Some day that money will be paid back, but I am reminded of a remark made by someone following the last war. The Russians were starving and some one assured them that they would have a good harvest in the spring. We may be able to wait for some years for the repayment of this money if, like the Russians, we* do not starve to death in the meantime. This net income of $2,636 is the best position in the series I am going to mention. That is the amount left to the member to permit him to live in Ottawa for six months and to maintain himself in his constituency for twelve months and pay the various expenses, including those of regular elections.
If he were a married man he would receive $2,636, but if he were single be would receive $2,406, after paying a tax of $1,594. That is what he would have left to maintain himself. I hope that there are few in this house, although I know there are some, who have to maintain themselves on what is left of their sessional indemnities after their taxes have been paid.
Let us suppose that someone with an income of $3,000 is waited upon by the usual committees urging him to become a member of parliament. Let us suppose that he consents and that he is unfortunate enough to be elected. Let us suppose something which is not always the case, that he is able to retain his income of $3,000. What will be his position?
On his income of $3,000 he would pay an income tax of $884. The expenses of being a member of parliament are offset with an indemnity of $4,000. When the $4,000 is added to the $3,000 he is placed in the $7,000 class, in which case his tax will be, not $884 but $2,985. That is to say, his tax will be increased by $2,101 by reason of his receiving the $4,000 indemnity. After the increased tax has been paid, he will have left out of his $4,000 the sum only of $1,899. That is the situation facing hon. members of this house.
The indemnity is paid not as a salary. It was instituted in the first instance to pay the expenses and thus make it possible for a poor man to be a member of parliament. In this case the indemnity is $1,899 and not $4,000.
Let us go into some of the slightly higher brackets. Supposing the man who is urged to become a member of parliament receives an income of 86,000 a year. Let us suppose that he becomes a member and is able to retain that income. With his indemnity his total income is now $10,000 and he goes into the $10,000 class. What are the figures? In the first instance, he would pay $2,415 on his income of $6,000, but when he goes into the $10,000 class by reason of his added expenses and added revenue, he will pay $4,762. The increase in taxation by reason of the receipt of the $4,000 will be $2,347. That is to say, he will retain out of the $4,000 only $1,653.
If one considers the expense of living in Ottawa for six months in the year and possibly maintaining a house, he can see that many members will be in the red. The hon. member for York-Sunbury confessed that he was in the red so far as his indemnity was concerned. I can match him in that. I, too, am in the red. By the time I have paid my living expenses in Ottawa, without figuring the time spent or the other expenses of my constituency and that sort of thing, I find
Income War Tax

that I am. out of pocket. That is, after I have paid my income tax out of the $4,000, it actually costs me. money to live in this city as a member of parliament, just to room and eat.
I am not speaking on my own behalf. I have no complaint to make with regard to the position I hold. I am intensely grateful to the constituency which paid me this honour and charged me with this responsibility, but I suggest to the committee this thought. The indemnity was established in the first instance in order that democracy might continue. It was the Labour mind of the House of Commons in England that advocated payment of members of parliament. It was not the rich who put it across; it was rather the poor. It was those classes who had public things in mind, and who knew that the poor man could not sit in the house unless his expenses were paid. The people of England came to realize that if the public did not pay, then somebody else would. It was in order to substitute the public man, in its truest sense, for that man who holds a seat in the house for the purpose of serving private interest that the public decided to pay the members' way. It was to substitute democracy for the service of private interest, that caused the English people to give an indemnity to their members of parliament.
The principle is as strong to-day as it was then. If we are to maintain democracy of this house, its high standing in the community and the respect of our fellow men, it is necessary to take this problem into consideration. If the administration feels that this is not the proper time to make a change, it should at all events lay this question before the electors at the next election, and see to it that the impression now abroad that members of parliament grow rich is dispelled. It is not true. Members of parliament grow poor in the service of the public, and our public does not know it. Let it be stated openly and publicly, boldly and without reservation, to the people of Canada and let them be told what is involved in this matter. If you continue the present policy you will restrict parliament to representatives of rich interests, to rich men and to people without responsibility who can live here on less than $3,000 a year.
The issue is clearly put. It is a financial issue. It is necessary in. order to preserve the strength, the credit, the respect of this house that we put our members in a position to pay their way, to be independent of anybody, to look the world in the face and say: "I owe not any man. I am not to be paid and I am not to be bought. I cannot be hired. My expenses cannot be paid by anybody. They are paid by my constituents, by the taxpayers of Canada, and I have but one

duty, the service of the people." I hope that my language has not been driving language. I hope that I have not urged this matter too strongly, because it is a subject for clear thought rather than of emotionalism. The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) suggested that we members did not have the courage with which to approach the question.

No; I
asked them to have courage.

All right. I am corrected to that extent. But it has not been lack of courage on our part that this matter has not been raised before. It has been a sense of responsibility. It has been that diffidence to advocate our own cause. It has been a readiness to sacrifice in order that this war might be carried on and that public morale might be maintained. It is a matter of credit to us and not of discredit that this question has not been previously discussed.
As for the Minister of Finance and the suggestion that he is anaemic in thought or lacks courage, let me ask how many in this house would like to substitute for him and to answer the barrage that meets him from both sides of the house, while he carries the responsibility of the raising of billions of dollars. I do not always agree with the Minister of Finance, but I have hfeld my peace knowing the burden that he carries. I have felt that he was not anaemic but rather a lion-heart-in his office.
Just one word on another subject that is related to the one before the house, namely, the abolition of the savings portion of the present income tax. Lest the Minister of Finance and the country think the criticism voiced is the general opinion, because of silence on the part of others, let me express commendation. Many of my fellow members feel that the administration deserves credit for making this change. There is such a thing as riding a willing horse to death. Statesmen must be careful not to go too far in bleeding a country white even in time of war. Caution in going too far and taking too much is wisdom at the present time. The abolition of this tax is intensely popular in the country.
It has been observed on the floor of the house that the change will benefit most strongly those in the lower 'income brackets, because those in the higher income brackets usually are able to offset a portion of the compulsory savings by the payment of insurance premiums and various other'things. It is the low income taxpayers who will benefit. I appreciate the argument that it is a good thing to have money now in order that we may have it to expend after the war is over. But you must take the whole financial policy

together. You must not select single points and emphasize them. While the poorer people will not save as much to expend after the war if this change goes into effect, on the other hand, if the present plans as I understand them are carried out, there will be family allowances. Something like $200,000,000 a year of purchasing power is to be distributed among the low income people of our country in the form of family allowances, thoroughly offsetting the loss of compulsory savings. One offsets the other. Both would give added purchasing power after the war. We now lose the compulsory savings, but on the other hand we gain $200,000,000 in family allowances.
The Minister of Finance has stated this afternoon that this question of indemnities has not been brought up in the house before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I did not say that. I asked the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard how many members had mentioned it on the floor of the house before. I did not mean to intimate that none had. He was representing that the discussion this afternoon showed a general movement of hon. members in favour of freeing part of their indemnity from taxation, and I asked him how many members [DOT] had brought it up before.

I wish to tell the minister that on three previous occasions this very question has been brought up in the house, once by myself, twice by my room-mate, the hon. member for Northumberland, New Brunswick, not Northumberland in the hills. The hon. member's contention was-and I think it is well founded-that the indemnity is paid to members of parliament to indemnify them for their time, and that under the House of Commons Act to consider this a salary is entirely improper-
And unconstitutional.

-and that if the legal lights could get together they might prove that every act of this parliament was illegal, because under the present taxation system we are put into the position of being employees of the government, and the House of Commons Act definitely states that a member of this house cannot be an employee of the government, with the exception of a soldier, sailor or airman serving his country during time of war. That is a very important point, and one which I think should be cleared up.
With regard to two hon. and gallant members who have intimated, I think quite publicly, that they could not afford to continue

to be members, I support the contention of the hon. members for Fraser Valley and for Northumberland, Ontario, that the loss of these two members to this country is a serious loss, and represents the sort of thing which may happen all across Canada. I say to the committee through you, Mr. Chairman, that in politics as in everything else you get what you pay for.
There is what I consider to be a particularly mean decision of the treasury board through which both of these hon. and gallant members suffer severely. I know this because I was fortunate enough to be serving overseas with one of them. By a ruling of the treasury board, if you are a member of this house you are not entitled to dependents' allowance; that is, separation allowance. That decision may be legal, but I suggest that it is very mean. It does not affect me now, but it did. I mention it now because it does not affect me. Here we have members -who, because they are such, are penalized, in that if they are married or get married their wives do not receive the separation allowance. It is a penalty illustrative of the mentality of the treasury board in its reaction to the matter of indemnities paid to members of this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is news to me. I discussed it with members, and certainly I am very much surprised. May I ask the hon. member, on what is the ruling based? It may be that it exists; it may be that it is validly based, but would the hon. gentleman give me a little enlightenment on that?
Yes. If you are in the army you get what is called a separation allowance for your wife.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The dependents' allowance.
The dependents' allowance. If you happen to be a member of the house that is automatically cut off, by the ruling of the treasury board, because you cannot draw a salary from two departments at once.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What about your soldier's pay?

You get that, but not while serving as a member of the house. I want to make this very clear, that no hon. member on active service while serving in this house draws two indemnities. He does not draw his army pay and his indemnity as a member of this house if he serves in this house.

While he is in the house.

He receives leave without pay to look after his parliamentary duties. But whether he is serving overseas or anywhere else he does not receive separation allowance for his wife at any time. I think that is a peculiarly picayune and rather mean proviso of the treasury board. I must say that it is not endearing the treasury board to those who are affected by it.
Which does he receive, his army pay or his parliamentary pay?

He receives his parliamentary pay in full. His wife gets no separation allowance from his army pay, and he loses his army pay while he is here in the House of Commons. I think that is the correct statement.
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Supposing he were here for six months he would receive his full parliamentary indemnity and no army pay during that period. During the remaining six months he could draw his army pay.
I think that is so. But he gets no wife's allowance at any time.

He would draw no separation allowance at any time. Both these hon. and gallant members have brought this up to me and mentioned it as peculiarly unfair and "small". Both of them are professional men, and married. Before they became members of parliament they lived on the fees which they received for their professional services. That source of income is completely cut off; both of them have found it almost impossible to live, and both have stated that they cannot remain members under these conditions. Because of the ruling I have mentioned we are losing from this house the very type of young men we should have in it.
I wish now to refer to the British budget. As brought down quite recently by Sir John Anderson, it definitely recognizes, or so I understand from the press, that a member of parliament has definite expenses, and gives him an allowance for them. Surely we can follow the lead given in this respect by the British house.
I hold in my hand a bill which shows that the Australian parliament recognizes not only the expenses which have been mentioned, but election expenses as well. I think the committee would be interested in one of the clauses of this act, since we are likely to have an election, I understand, in the very near future. Section 74 of the Australian income tax assessment act as revised this year reads:
[Mr. It. B. Hanson.3
Expenditure incurred in the year of income by .the taxpayer in being elected as a member, or in contesting an election for membership, of the parliament or of the parliament of a state shall be allowable deduction.
That is a very interesting clause, and remember it is put in by a Labour government. I think it is important for this reason. What we have to do in Canada is to see to it that the type of man we get in the House of Commons is truly representative of the people throughout the countiy. We are going to be faced with a good many young men coming back, discharged and demobilized; we hope that the next House of Commons will have a great number of servicemen in it, and unless we liberalize our methods of taxation and our present method of reducing the indemnity until it is impossible to live on it, we are not going to get, after the next election, the type of independently thinking young man in the House of Commons that we should have. Everything should be done under our taxation policy to make it easy for courageous and forceful young men who have fought for their country to become condidates for parliamentary honour. We need that type of young man, but under the present taxation system we do everything to discourage such men, and that is one of my most serious condemnations of the present system.
Several matters have been brought up on this resolution and I wish to say just one word with regard to succession duties.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When the committee took recess at six o'clock, I was speaking in general terms about the peculiar way in which we as Canadians treat our public men. There is in Canada a philosophy, I think one of the most pernicious that could be harboured in any country, that all men who go into public life do so for ulterior reasons; and when a public man is defeated many people continue to bear a personal dislike to that individual. No other country in the world treats its public servants as badly as Canada does. To-day there are living in Canada I think seven gentlemen who at one time or another have been premiers of some of the sovereign provinces of this dominion. All or most of them are living in a degree of oblivion; some have been or perhaps are actually close to destitution. That is something the public man sees in Canada when he looks around. He sees men once great, once leaders of great provinces, elected

Income War Tax
by the public will, whom the fortunes of politics have turned down and who have been treated worse than men engaged in any other line of endeavour. These are the things we see, and they are not conducive to the wellbeing of the state.
We have taken a cynical attitude toward public servants. We have said that no man who enters the public service can possibly be honest. That is the philosophy of the country. When I was elected to this house I was in the army. My colonel said to me, "If you had been in the penitentiary for five years people would have forgotten and forgiven you. Now you have become a politician, and that will stay with you for the rest of your life." That is the philosophy we have spread in Canada, and I say to hon. members that it is a damnable philosophy. We do not consider, as do the English and the other democracies, that a man enters the public service of his country for the same reasons that another man enters the armed service of his country. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that until we overcome these peculiar ideas we shall continue to have the sort of negative government we have at the present time. That is all I have to say with regard to the sessional indemnity.
I should now like to say a word about succession duties, which I believe come under this item. There is a specific item dealing with them, but what I have to say is more germane to this item than to any other. It is a peculiar thing, but we have developed the philosophy that it is a sin to make a success of anything. Once a man has made a success in life he is considered suspect, and the taxing authorities of this dominion regard his estate almost as an enemy of the country. I bow to your ruling, of course, Mr. Chairman; but since this afternoon the general subjects of the functions of chartered banks and the Bank of Canada, and the issue of debt-free money were allowed, I considered' that on the first item there would be an opportunity to all members to discuss the general taxation policy. Mr. Chairman, so far as possible I shall endeavour to confine my remarks to the first item in the resolutions. I believe it is quite in order that we discuss the taxation upon the sessional indemnities of members of parliament. I must point out that I have a great deal of sympathy with my fellow members in the matter of taxation of those indemnities, and I cannot see any rhyme or reason why a member of parliament is not entitled to the legitimate expenses connected' with his being a member of parliament as would be enjoyed by any other Canadian citizen. Some consideration should1 ibe given to that aspect of the situation. We are taxed on the full amount of our sessional indemnity, and I myself find considerable difficulty in paying

those -taxes. Like the hon. member for York-Sunbury, I find that SI ,400 is deducted from my S4,000 indemnity for income tax. However, I do not expect to go into the red, because in the past I have tried to conduct my business affairs so that this will not happen, if at all possible.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury complained about the high cost of living. If it requires as much to live as he said it does, then perhaps it is a case of the cost of living high, so far as that hon. member is concerned.
But when it comes to the point of increasing our sessional indemnities by rewarding members of parliament and giving them a monetary consideration commensurate with their positions, I am not so sure that this is an appropriate approach to the problem. First, I was nominated as a Liberal candidate in my riding, the constituency of Brant. When I was nominated and elected I knew the indemnity was $4,000. I did not have to take part in the election; this was still a free country. But I have found there are many who, like myself, are anxious to make some contribution to the public service. After listening to some hon. members who spoke this afternoon, one might decide that they were giving their time and attention without any remuneration at all. The indemnity might not be as large as some think it should be; while the House of Commons is as fairly representative a cross-section of the people as can be found, it is still possible that some of the 245 members may not be worth even the $4,000, and would not make that if they had to compete in some other form of life. That is a point which should be considered.
After all, the average member of parliament has a contribution to make when he offers his services at election time. Very often during the campaign his speeches reflect a high plane of thought, when he solicits the votes of his constituents to support him in the contribution he wishes to make to the public service.
There are other compensations besides the monetary one. The first of these is the honour of being a member of parliament-because I consider it a great honour to represent the people of Brant. I have had many predecessors whom I have looked upon with much approval.

You cannot eat
honour.

I did not hear the hon. member. The fact is that some most honoured men have represented the constituency of Brant, and I feel highly honoured in being one of those called upon to represent those

splendid people. That is a consideration which money cannot buy, and which should be kept in mind.
If one places only a monetary value upon his membership in the House of Commons,, then we see at once that there are some in the house who, in many other walks of life,, might earn four or five times as much as they receive here as members of parliament. So that I suggest the matter should not be considered only from a monetary point of view. After all, the member of parliament has a contribution he can make, one which I believe is best exemplified in a book I take a great deal of pleasure in reading, when I want inspiration. This book is called "Self-Help," by Samuel Smiles, and at one page I find this:
Even the humblest person, who sets before his fellows an example of industry, sobriety, and upright honesty of purpose in life, has a present as well as a future influence upon the well-being of his country; for his life and character pass unconsciously into the lives of others, and propagate good example for -all time to come.
If we as members of parliament, in the dying hours of a session, say that we are going to extract more from the taxpayers of this country, I am wondering what kind of example that would be to our fellowmen.
After all, there is this to be said about it, that in these days in which our boys are fighting against tyranny a weapon has been put into the hands of civilians, namely, the weapon of taxation. That weapon is evidenced in various types of controls, price-freezing, pricesetting, gasoline rationing, sugar rationing, and controls of other kinds. Many of these controls can be used as weapons in the hands of civilians. I am sorry to say I have had complaints from some who have been too cowardly to use those controls with a grace which would have been commensurate with the contribution being made by our soldiers.
This is a weapon we have within our hands,, and we must use it to help our boys when they are fighting the forces of tyranny; because, after all, they could not get very far if we as civilians did not back them up. I repeat that when I hear people complain of high taxes, I am bound to remember that we are living in a country which is free, one in which our homes are not bombed, and one in which we enjoy many privileges. We complain of some of the weapons the Minister of Finance is using, the taxation he is inflicting upon us, but I consider it is the right and privilege of a citizen to pay these taxes. We should not overlook that.
It would be unfortunate if we as members-of parliament showed a bad example at this

particular time. I hesitate to think where it might end. Naturally we all do not like paying taxes; but if we as members of parliament (Jo not show our sense of duty, how can we expect those who are fighting our battles for $1.50 a day to react? What will they think of members of parliament who are looking after their own particular interests regardless of the welfare of our soldiers who are fighting our battles at this particular time? I may be all wrong-
You certainly are.
The hon. member is quite within his right to pass his opinion. I may be all wrong, but I have never reached the point where I consider I never make a mistake.
You never will.

There are those who claim they never make mistakes, but they do not know when they make one. I am not so sure that making it easy for society will produce the best results. There are those who have -admitted that they have enjoyed the fruits of poverty in their success. I should like to quote again from the same book:
Riches and. ease, it is perfectly clear, are not necessary for man's highest culture, else had not the world been so largely indebted in all times to those who have sprung from the humbler ranks. An easy and luxurious existence does not train men to effort or encounter with difficulty; nor does it awaken that consciousness of power which is so necessary for energetic and effective action in life.
We have in this house men who have deserted a particular field to come and work for this poverty-stricken indemnity of $4,000 that is taxed. We do not seem to have any difficulty in finding people to take this truck-driver's job. Truck-driver's pay was mentioned this afternoon, but I do not think that kind of phraseology lends dignity to this house. I do not want to get on too high a plane but, after all, I feel that a member of parliament should set an exemplary example in his community.
Some of those who have spoken have referred to the lack of fortitude and courage on the part of the Minister of Finance in facing this issue. Some of us who come from the simpler walks of life do not feel as strongly about this matter as others. So far as I am concerned, if some of these gentlemen do not think the $4,000 indemnity is sufficient there is no reason why they should not resign their seats and put their energies to other things where they may be better rewarded.
I would be much opposed to increasing the indemnity at a time like this without asking for the confidence of the people whom I have the honour to represent. While it is an
honour to be a member of parliament, it is only right that the member of parliament should deserve that honour and not take advantage of an opportunity to increase his monetary remuneration at a time when the country is struggling so hard. There are people who think we are already getting too much. I believe a service has been rendered to the people of Canada by directing attention to the position in which a member of parliament finds himself to-day.
On page 32 of the appendix to the budget there is a table showing the percentage distribution of estimated revenues and expenditures. One heading covers legislation, which I understand includes the indemnities of senators and members of parliament and the salaries of all officials associated with the two houses. I find that the percentage of the expenditure for legislation is -05 per cent of the total. This is just a bagatelle compared with other expenditures. Of course .war expenditures were the greatest, being 86-28 per cent. However, the principle is still there, and I do not think we have the right to increase our own remuneration.
