I would not have taken part in this debate but for the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wood) who has just sat down. I would not go so far as to say that I -resent them for, of course, he is entitled to his views. But I deprecate them; perhaps that is the better word. Of course, every member and every section of this house and of this country have their own troubles. The hon. member occupies a seat apparently reasonably close to this city which allows him to go home week-ends. There are members of this house who are known as the Thursday-Tuesday people, who disappear at 3.30 p.m. on Thursday and we do not see them again until 10.30 on Tuesday night. They can go home over a long week-end and conduct their business in some kind of way at any rate by this week-end supervision. But those of us who come from the far west are tied down here for the whole session. If the session meets in November there is not time enough 
to make it worth while going home at Christmas. If I had gone home at Easter I would have had exactly two days at home. So that we who come from the far west are tied down here from the beginning of the session to whatever time the powers that be or the lap of the gods decide that we can go home. That makes a difference. I conducted a fairly profitable little business which I had to sell because I could not get home to run it.
Anything I have to say, Mr. Chairman, will come with better grace from myself than from some other members because it is well known that I am not going to run again. Therefore I shall be free of any suggestion such as the hon. member for Brant made that perhaps members had a personal and a pecuniary interest in suggesting that some adjustment should be made in connection with our expenses. It can mean nothing to me. I am only trying to put forward my views for the benefit of those who will come after me and, as I hope to show, for the benefit of the country.
The country will lose a good servant if you do not come back.
I hope it may be my pleasure in time to come to look down on this assembly and see how it is progressing.
It will be nice to have you still with us.

It is quite true, as the hon. member for Brant said, that nobody asked us to run. On the other hand, the people who sent us here expect us to fight for their rights and privileges, and we have not the courage to fight for our own. If we have rights, surely we are entitled to them.
Somebody says that an adjustment has not been asked for to-day. I will take it upon myself now to ask, on behalf of those members who may come after me, that there should be, not an increase in the indemnity, but fair treatment as regards members' expense accounts. I hope that by putting it on the record it may get out to the public, because many people are entirely ignorant of the real facts. The popular idea is that we live here at the expense of the country. When people read in the papers, for instance, that the restaurant went several thousand dollars behind, they think we got the benefit of all that. We do not. A good many people think we do not pay for our lodgings here and so on. A gentleman, a very decent fellow, once sent me a wire collect. It was a nice chatty wire, beginning, "Dear Mr. Neill" and ending with "Yours sincerely". It cost me $7.50. He thought that was one of my privileges.

Income War Tax
I only ask that we should be treated the same as any other body. Many years ago- I may be wrong in this, but this is my impression from studying the thing at the time-the same question arose in more modified form, and the then Minister of Finance, I think it was Mr. Fielding, but it might have been his predecessor, said that he would arrange it so that members would get some allowance for their expenses.
If I were a real estate agent I would be allowed, when making up my income tax return, to deduct from my profits any expenses that I had incurred in obtaining those profits. I have to maintain an office, rent, fuel, light, telephone, et cetera, and a stenographer all the time to carry on my political work. If I were a lawyer or a doctor I would be allowed to deduct those expenses from my income, and quite properly so. There is no occupation that would not be allowed to do that. But we are not. There is no sense of fairness about that. It does not make common sense.
Some seventeen years ago, being Scotch, and the Scotch can always see a nickel without a microscope, I took up this question with an authority in the taxation branch. The difference was not nearly as great then as it is now. I said to him, "I am entitled to deduct these expenses." He said, "No, you are not." I said, "Oh, yes; here it is in the law. It says that if you are away from home pursuing your business or occupation you can deduct your expenses. If I had been in the contracting business I could deduct my travelling expenses." But he said, "No, you cannot deduct your expenses." Then I said, "How do you get around that- sentence in the law? Is not my business as a member of parliament an occupation?" He said, "No, it is not." Then I said, "What is it?" And he said, "It is an honour." And for that honour I have to pay all these expenses out of my own pocket. That was seventeen years ago.
The question was raised again more recently because the pressure of taxation brought it home to hon. members. Some of them consulted a high official in the taxation branch and he laughed at them. He said, "Of course, you are entitled to make the deduction, but you have been standing for it for so long that it would not look well to make a change now just before an election."
Two years ago I brought this question up on the legislation items in the estimates, which I thought was the proper place, but I got no support, and I left the house rather disgusted. I met some members and said to them, "You know blamed well I was right, why didn't you
back me up?" They said, "That's all very well for you, Neill, but you are not going to run again and we are."
The government has been accused of a lack of courage. The blame is not altogether the government's. It is the members who did not have the courage to demand what was coming to them. They were afraid of public sentiment. It is not good to be afraid of public sentiment. The fear is wholly misplaced in this case. The common people, the working people, the union people never want their members to be cheap. The idea of doing something cheap will not get anywhere with them, and they will always stand for a reasonable explanation.
An election was coming off in Nova Scotia some years ago, and the government of the day, in order to popularize themselves, just as our hon. friend opposite had in his mind perhaps, reduced their salaries by two or three hundred dollars. The next day the newspapers came out with great big headlines-I remember one paper, a Labour paper had this headline: "Legislators cut down their salaries." But the next line read: "Cheap Skates! They knew what they were worth." That is all the applause they got from the working man. The working man wants good wages for himself, and he is willing that those who do good service for others shall get paid for it.
I remember once talking to a group of working men along the same lines. It was at a logging camp. I said that I was not being paid enough and that I would vote for an increase. One of the men said, "You say that you are not getting paid enough. Then why do you run? Nobody asked you to run." "That is perfectly true," I said, "but the reason I run is the same reason that brings some of you to town to get drunk. I get a kick out of it, whether I get paid properly for it or not." I would love to run again, but the state of my health forbids it. Let me tell the committee that I might not be so frank if I were running again; I would be accused of ulterior motives; but I am thinking of the people who are coming after me, good men who may be prevented from running because of existing conditions.
Last year I kept a fairly close record of my expenses. Everyone who knows me-my fellow members and my neighbours at home

know I live in a very quiet way. When a man works thirteen hours a day he has not much time for a frivolous life. My hours at home are eight a.m. to ten p.m., with an hour off at noon, and that does not leave me much time to go in for riotous living. So that I live quietly and inexpensively. But I was just $575 out by being a member of parliament last
Income War Tax

year. I must say that I included in my expenses the sum of $1,000 toward my election expenses, because that generally costs me between four and five thousand dollars, and each year I take off a thousand dollars of my indemnity to make up that amount. Even at that I would be glad to go on doing it, for the honour of it; as I say, it is the only job I know; it has been my recreation and my hobby, as well as my occupation for twenty-eight years.
There is just one other point I wish to make. If we go on the way we are doing a new system will develop ; indeed it is developing now. The hon. member who sits behind me said that he knew of two members who for that reason were not going to run, and certainly there are other members who will be deterred on the same grounds from standing again. I asked a man whom I know if he would run to take my place. He had very good qualifications, but he lacked private means. He said that he would have been *willing to stand, but he could not afford it; he had a wife and family. Here is what we are going to develop-and heaven forbid that it should come in Canada: we are going to have a parliament of rich men or the stooges of rich men; it will be either one or the other. The rich man can afford to be a member of parliament; and perhaps would desire to be one, wholly from a sense of honour and responsibility; nevertheless he is a rich man and, when it comes down to the point, he looks at things through the eyes of the rich man. The poor man looks at things through the eyes of the poor man. Either you are going to have rich men who can afford to be out of pocket, or poor men who will be tools of rich men or companies or interests. It does not necessarily have to be engineered by some company; there may be nothing actually improper; but the man who pays the piper sets the tune, and the man or interest that finances a campaign will have an awful lot to say about its policies.
I therefore think that the proposed change would be a fair thing. I do not ask for any increase of indemnity, although it may be remarked that in the United States their representatives are paid far more, but simply that every member should be entitled to deduct his legitimate expenses, and I would not put them at a high figure so that the system could be abused. Let the allowance for expeness be a reasonable one, taking account of the fact that a man may have to give up his business, as we in British Columbia have to do. I would ask any lawyers from British Columbia what their businesses are worth to-day. This would

be fair for business and good for democracy. I submit also that it would be a good thing for the people, who want to be represented not by rich men or by stooges but by people just like themselves who can afford to come and represent them. I hope the minister will take some cognizance of the suggestion to make some allowance for expenses legitimately incurred, as we all know they must be. I do not believe the government would suffer by it, and I do not think any hon. member who suggests it or votes for it will suffer either, because the people are sound, commonsensible folk, who do not want any more than is coming to them, and they want everyone to get a square deal.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to surprise -you and also the minister, because I intend to speak on an item. We have been almost four hours on this subject, and I think we should get on an item, unless the minister would like to speak first.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should like to speak some time on this question of taxation of members' indemnities.
Speak now, then.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Perhaps before the minister speaks I may be permitted to say a few words. The reason why I ask the privilege of speaking first is that I should like to anticipate one argument he may use, in case one of the interjections which the parliamentary assistant made this afternoon reflects some of the thinking of the minister. I do not hold it against the parliamentary assistant for the interjection he made; he may have been provoked by the nature of the remarks at that moment; but what he said was something like this, if I remember correctly, "It is very nice to be relieving ourselves of taxation." If I felt that that was what we were asking for I should be opposed to any such move, just as other hon. members have stated their opposition to an increase in the amount of the indemnity. But what I feel we are doing here to-day is directly in line with the third basic consideration which the minister outlined in his budget speech. As reported in Hansard, at page 4174, he said:
A third consideration is the desirability of relieving cases of special hardship which very frequently arise when tax rates are heavy, and of removing some anomalies which experience has revealed in the working of our laws.
I would say to the minister and the parliamentary assistant that under the terms of that consideration members of parliament, by

Income War Tax
correspondence, by interviews with the minister, by raising cases in the house, have fought hard in connection with a number of anomalies and conditions which they considered unfair and unjust. The minister, in the very speech to which I have referred, made announcements to take care of a number of these anomalies. Let me take a moment to refer to some of them. First there is the proposed change with regard to undue medical expenses, so that the amount over five per cent is now allowable as an exemption, whether expended in Canada or the United States. He made a new provision with regard to the expenses of the blind. He brought illegitimate children and in-laws into the exemption classes. He made provision for exemption in the case of payments of alimony. He suggested a new provision with respect to the maintenance of self-contained domestic establishments.
There are some other matters which the minister has not adjusted as yet, such as meeting a request which hon. members have made for an exemption to parents of student nurses. There was also the matter which I mentioned the other night, namely, that of granting sleeping-car conductors and sleeping-car porters the same away-from-home expense allowance which is allowed to brakemen, firemen, engineers and train conductors.
The point I am trying to make is that in connection with all these cases what members of parliament on all sides of the house have fought for is not relief from taxation; what they have fought for is equity, for an adjustment of what they considered anomalies; and I feel, quite frankly, that we are only at this stage of the game doing something on behalf of ourselves which we have done strenuously on behalf of those whom we represent.
I know that in our own group, when we were discussing this matter one day, my colleague the hon. member for Cape Breton South made the comment that if a case similar to that of members of parliament were brought to our attention from outside the house we would rise in this chamber and fight like the mischief on behalf of such people. So that I do not think we are asking for any concession or any relief from taxation; we are simply asking that the third consideration which the minister laid down in his budget speech should be thought of as applying to these cases.
A .number of sets of figures relative to this matter were given to the minister to-day. I was interested in the figures given by the hon. member for Trinity, but other figures might be added! to those, because he gave the figures for a member who has another income before he comes here, one which is still his
after he becomes a member. There are some of us here who, whatever the reason may be, have no other source of income once we are elected. I am not complaining at all, I am quite satisfied, I may say to the hon. member for Brant and others. Even if no adjustment is made, or even if the taxes are increased, I intend, so long as the electors of Winnipeg North Centre are satisfied, to continue coming here as a member of parliament. I wish to render such service as I can in this capacity, so that there is nothing in the nature of a threat or a promise, as my political opponents might suggest, in this connection. However, may I state, my own case. Apart from any profession I may have followed, I am a member of the International Typographical Union. If I were working at the trade as a linotype operator in Winnipeg, working at the present scale of wages, subject to the taxation now in effect, living in Winnipeg, and having only one home to maintain, it would leave me better off financially than I am under present circumstances. Once again let me say I am not complaining. But I do feel that just as on the one hand I do not want to be better off than the people whom I represent, because of my work as a member of parliament, so I know that the people whom I represent do not want me to be worse off than I would be if I had not gone in for public service in this way. I think the minister should take into consideration the case of members who give their full time and have no other income, as well as cases of the kind referred to by the hon. member for Trinity.
Speaking of interjections, I thought I heard the minister interject at one point that he doubted whether in the past, at some stage of the game, there had been very great unanimity in the house on this matter. If that was so in the past, one of the reasons I am speaking tonight, although as a matter of fact the position of this party was sufficiently well stated by our leader, is to add, what I feel the minister should realize now, that there is practical unanimity on this point. That does not mean that in the view of some of us it was ever right that some consideration along the line we are now urging should not have been given. It simply bears out the correctness of what the minister said in that sentence to which I have referred, that when tax rates are heavy some of these anomalies are brought to light. With the experience of laws of this kind there are revealed things that were not caught before; and because of that experience, because of the way the tax rates operate, members feel the justice of putting up this fight for themselves, comparable with the fight which we
Income War Tax

have put up for others, and to which the minister in many cases has responded. There is great unanimity at the present time. In fact, I believe the committeee is unanimous; the only member who has offered any reservations having been the hon. member for Brant; But even he did not oppose the suggestion that there should1 be some adjustment along this line, and I hope that factor, if it was one that was sticking in the minister's mind, will now be taken into consideration by him, namely, that all parties in the house, members on all sides, are agreed1 that it is a just' request which we are making.

I have no regrets for having brought up this matter to-day, and I do not believe that I have in any way overstated the position. I was rather disturbed at an interjection made by the parliamentary assistant, to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has referred, because the parliamentary assistant intimated that it was nice for us to relieve ourselves from income taxation. On reflection I do not think he will persist in that position. I do not believe there has been any disposition on the part of anyone to benefit oneself in the course of this debate to-day. Certainly I made no claim for relief myself. I want to make that abundantly clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not understand that.
I understand that what the hon. gentleman suggests, and what many others have suggested, would relieve members of parliament from many hundreds of dollars of income taxation.

That may be the effect of it, but that was not the motive underlying my position. I am quite content to pay income tax. I have paid it from the beginning and I expect to pay it until I die, but I want to pay only on true income, and members of parliament are not paying on true income. That is the difficulty which the minister has not met.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not spoken.

Well, I
know the minister must have had this matter under consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why, certainly.
The government must have had it under consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For years.

I am informed that it has been the subject-matter of discussion within the party itself. I will not go farther than that. It has not borne

so hardly until the war, until the high rates have come into effect, and then it has come home to hon. members that they are being taxed on their gross income without allowance whatever being given to the cost of procuring that income. The net is what should be taxed. I have had this matter up with the department. The department took the view that parliament itself has the remedy and I am trying to get parliament to apply the remedy. I do not want anyone to take from any remarks I made this afternoon that I was advocating an increase in indemnity; I am not. I am asking the government to put the taxation of parliamentary indemnities on the true basis, exactly on the same basis that they put me as a practising lawyer, where I charge for postage stamps. A practising lawyer charges up every item of expense- telegraph and telephone tolls, rentals, and so on; every time he has to move, travelling expenses are charged up. Nobody could earn income on any other basis if he did not do it in the way I have suggested. But a member of parliament, because of lack of courage of members of parliament in the past-I can only put it in that way-is now legislated into a position which is not only an anomaly but much worse than that. It is cruel to members of parliament to tax them on their expenses in earning their sessional indemnity.
I take a constitutional view of this question, and if it were fought I do not think these indemnities would be regarded as income. I know the only case that has been tried in Canada was one in reference to the salary of a lieutenant governor where it was held that the expenses of the lieutenant governor in entertaining, owing to the position he occupied, were disallowed. The expenses which a member of parliament has to incur are on an entirely different plane.
I should like to impress upon the Minister of Finance and the other members of the government that members of parliament do not object to paying income tax on true income. They do object to paying income tax on gross income, without any allowance for the cost of earning that income. Could I state it in any shorter form than that? That is the principle upon which I base my objection. I did not offer any suggestion this afternoon as to quantum, nor do I now. I suggest that consideration should be given by the government to this whole problem. If they do not want to put it into effect for this parliament, put it into effect for the next one, so that this thing which has rankled in the breasts of members of parliament for twenty-three years, to my own personal knowledge, and about which they have been afraid to move for fear

Income War Tax
of criticism, may be rectified. I ask for justice for members of parliament. I am not asking justice for myself in that regard. It does not matter a bit to me; I may not be back in this house. But I should like to see my successor, to whatever party he may belong, who may be a man without private means, in a better position. How can he leave his business in Fredericton, come here for six months of the year and maintain and educate his family as he is bound to do, on S4,000 a year, taxed at the rates in force to-day? The thing just does not add up to common decency, and certainly it is not democratic. I am sure my electors will support the position I have taken. I am sure the electors of this country, if they understand the position, will support any reasonable action taken by the government with respect to this matter. I should like to know of any other class of people in the country who are taxed on gross income. I do not know of any; none comes to mind at the moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are hundreds.

There may be, but none occurs to me at the moment. If there are others, that is another case of injustice, although of course each case has to be analysed and must stand on its own feet. The debate this afternoon has demonstrated the injustice of the present position, and the -government ought to pay heed to what has been said.

discouraged with the present situation that they feel their duty to their own families compels them to leave public life. At present, unless a man has made a fortune before coming here, or unless he has inherited some money, he cannot carry on. I submit to the minister that some way should be found to lighten the burden upon members of parliament, either by exempting from taxation a certain portion of the indemnity, or by allowing an hon. member to deduct the amount of his personal expenses here in Ottawa. Some way should be found to get around the difficulty.
According to what we have heard here today from members representing all provinces and all parties, such action should be well received by the people. I know some people say that this is the wrong time to do anything like this, while so many of our young men are making great sacrifices in connection with the war. Of course that has to be considered. It may be said that this would be a dangerous time to take such action, but I do not agree. When the time comes I am going to make the same representations in regard to the salaries of judges. I am glad to know that my remarks in that connection are in accord with views expressed by the labour unions, who have already passed a resolution stating that the judiciary should be able to carry on their duties without any fear of financial difficulty for themselves and their families. If I am not mistaken the same resolution also included members of parliament. So that it is encouraging to realize that at least in some quarters this situation has been recognized. I want to go on record as supporting what has been said in this connection to-day by members who have advocated that relief be granted one way or another to members.

I do not think I can add very much to what has already been said, but I wish to go on record as endorsing the proposals that have been advanced by the hon. member for York-Sunbury and others. However, I believe we should look at it perhaps a little differently from the point of view of the advantage it would be to members in the present house. After all, this session is pretty close to an end; I understand there will be an election before very long, so that there may be quite a change in the personnel of this house. Who are they to be? Are they to be the young men who have come home from overseas? Are they to be able to come here and represent their constituents-and probably represent the men alongside whom they have fought overseas? I doubt if they can possibly do so, because it is impossible to break even on the present indemnity.
The way I look at it is this: What class of men are we to have representing us in
TMr. Picard.]
Ottawa in the future? I think of my own riding, and many others, and then I think of the many young men I would like to see coming here to Ottawa, probably in preference to myself. They are welcome to it this time, and I would be glad to support a younger man. But I cannot ask them to take the risk, because there is not sufficient in it for them.
I wonder how many men in this house who have sons would recommend to them that they make politics their business with the present outlook in that career? Unless there is something more than just a living, I am sure we are not going to ask them to do it. And if we cannot ask our own sons to do it, are, we going to ask the sons of other people?
I probably spend more money than some. I know I come a long way from having anything left over, after paying for my accommodation and expenses while in Ottawa. Probably, as the hon. member for Brant has said, the high cost of living has something to do with my expenses; but let me tell the committee that last year I spent forty nights in a sleeping car-and I am not going to spend forty nights in an upper berth, or forty nights cramped up in a lower berth, either, if I can get a compartment. Therefore it cost me a considerable sum of money to come here and to return.
I do not think I am in the poor man's class, nor am I in the rich man's. But for the remainder of the time I have left to me, I think I am entitled to a little bit of comfort. Therefore I think, with the others, that some remedy should be brought about to enable young men to enter this life. When I think of the -hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) I think of a splendid example of what a man can do in public life, when he devotes his whole time to it. And as one of the three members from Vancouver island I regret very much that he has made a definite decision that he is not going to return to this chamber. I say that because the whole island of Vancouver will lose a very valuable servant.

As one of the more recent members to come to this chamber, and one who must live entirely on his indemnity, I think I should add a few words to those, already spoken. First, to make my position clear, as the hon. member for Brant pointed out, I was under no compulsion to accept the nomination for York South. I may say this, though, that men in that constituency who had given many years to public service-many more years than I had given- were offered the nomination I accepted, and reported themselves unable to accept because

Income War Tax
they could not educate their school-age families with what would be left of the indemnity they would receive by coming to Ottawa.
I, myself, would not have been willing to accept the nomination until I had reached an age in life when my family was educated, and as a result some of my family responsibilities had decreased. On what is left of my indemnity, I could not to-day maintain my home in Toronto, and rear and educate my family, and also at the same time pay my bills in Ottawa.
As the hon. member for Brant said, I realize there is some honour attached to being a member of parliament. Unfortunately, however, that honour is not legal tender in the commercial banks of our country.
Honour is greater than legal tender.

When I wish to make an instalment payment on the principal sum of a mortgage, or to make an interest payment, or when I wish to pay premiums on life insurance I find that those people insist upon being paid in something more than honour. I can understand that anyone who is in business or on a farm, a type of occupation which could be carried on just as profitably in his absence as when he is there, and from which he might receive an income, might possibly afford to live on what he gets at Ottawa.
But I did not come to public life from one of the better paid professions; I came from the lowly profession of schoolteaching. For twenty years I had worked in that profession, had gained promotion, and had reached a point where I was within a very few hundred dollars of being one of the best paid teachers in Canada. That was my position when I came to Ottawa. At that time I was receiving almost identically the nominal amount we receive as indemnity.
I find that living in Ottawa costs me a considerable amount of money. I am not attempting to overstate what I am saying, f am not like the hon. member for York-Sunbury, an ex-cabinet minister, and I have not yet reached the stage where I insist upon travelling in a compartment. But I find that, while receiving almost identically the same salary I received as a teacher, that salary is worth a thousand dollars a year less to me in Ottawa, as a member of parliament, than the same amount would have been to me as a schoolteacher in Toronto. That is the condition, living on the scale on which I live, in one room in Ottawa, and with most of my meals in the cafeteria, at thirty-five cents each.
In other words, I am paying taxes on at least a thousand dollars I never see, except
to pass it out in expenses which I am forced to incur by reason of my work here. And those additional expenses, together with expenses required to get around my riding- and probably to get around some other ridings [DOT]-are not taken into account.

My difficulty in considering this question is and has been- this will explain the interjection I made this afternoon-that the indemnities we are paid to provide for expenses existed in 1940 when I was elected'. What about the cost of living bonus?

It is for that reason that I am impressed with the suggestion thrown out by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, that whatever action we now see fit to take to correct our own position should be taken not for this parliament but for the next. Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two in order to associate myself with what has been said so ably by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, the hon. member for York-Sunbury, the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and others. I think they have made out an admirable case that relief should be given to members of parliament. I am concerned about the type of men who will be induced to run for parliament in the future. Reference has been made to the young men who are serving our country overseas and who will be returning home. Many of these men will be without occupation and some will have a flair and a desire for public service. Will they be able to afford to come to parliament? Will they be able to raise a family in decency, to educate their children and maintain themselves on the indemnity now given?
I would not ask for relief from taxation, but I think it ik improper to tax the expenses of members. I hope that no main will be prevented from entering public life for financial reasons. We do not want this house to be made up only of rich men. I think the quality of the house and of the legislation passed would suffer materially if that were the case. I hope that this house will be representative of every class in the community. We must make it possible for everyone in the community who wishes to do so to offer himself for public service. It is true that this is attended with a certain amount of honour, but the member should be free of financial worry if he is to do his duty to his constituents. We want to attract the best brains in the community to the House of Commons, and therefore I hope that the minister will consider the removal of taxation from money paid out in expenses.

Before the minister replies I should like to crave the

3. For the purposes of this act, "income" means the annual net profit or gain or gratuity, whether ascertained and capable of computation as being wages, salary, or other fixed amount, or unascertained as being fees or emoluments. . . .

(d) the salaries, indemnities or other remuneration of

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know whether there are other members who want to speak on this but I should like to deal with the matter myself at some length, perhaps for fifteen or twenty minutes, if not longer.
I want to make one thing very clear, that members of parliament and ministers, because ministers have been referred to in the discussion this afternoon and evening, are paid exactly what they were paid before the war and are taxed on exactly the same business on which they were taxed before the war. I want to make that very clear at the outset. The only difference in the treatment of members and ministers during the war and before the war is in the weight of taxation, the higher rates of taxation. There is no other difference either one way or the other in respect of either ministers or members. We are applying the same

Let me give the basis for the rule of taxing the salaries of members of parliament. It may be that this should be changed. That I am not arguing now. I am simply stating the facts because a lot of the facts have been overlooked in the discussion this afternoon and evening. Section 3 of the Income War Tax Act reads as follows:
3. For the purposes of this act, "income" means the annual net profit or gain or gratuity, whether ascertained and capable of computation as being wages, salary, or other fixed amount, or unascertained as being fees or emoluments, or as being profits from a trade or commercial or financial or other business or calling, directly or indirectly received by a person from any office or employment, or from any profession or calling, or from any trade, manufacture or business, as the case may be whether derived from sources within Canada or elsewhere; and shall include the interest, dividends or profits directly or indirectly received from money at interest, upon any security or without security, or from stocks, or from any other investment, and, whether such gains or profits are divided or distributed or not, and also the annual profit or gain from any other source including
(d) the salaries, indemnities or other remuneration of
(i) members of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada and officers thereof.
That has always been interpreted by the income tax division as meaning that when the taxation of wages or salary was being considered the wages or salary constituted the net profit or gain or gratuity which was being taxed, and that certainly applied to salaries, indemnities or other remuneration of members of the Senate and House of Commons and officers thereof.
Will the minister allow me? What effect does that ruling give to the word "net"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The word "net" applies to profit undoubtedly and if it is taken as applying to gain and gratuity, it is explained and defined by the following words, "whether ascertained and capable of computation as being wages, salary, or other fixed amount", in which event the net profit or gain or gratuity is ascertained. There is nothing more to be said about it. It is not to be increased or reduced. Then it goes on to say, "or unascertained", in which event one will have to look at the expenses and what it took to earn the income and so on.
Whether that is the correct legal interpretation or not, that is the interpretation which has been placed on that section uniformly ever since the section was enacted, and the income

tax division has been very, very careful not to permit from salaries a deduction for the expenses of earning the salary. They have had hundreds of thousands of claims in the course of their administration for just such expenses by persons, for instance, who have had to move from one place to another in order to take a position and who have claimed the removal expenses as part of the costs of earning the new salary; and claims from persons who find it inconvenient, impracticable, in some cases impossible to move their families from where they have been living to the situs of the new job and who have claimed the expenses which they have had to incur at the situs of the new job as expenses in earning the salary. There are multitudinous cases where claims have been put in by wage-earners and by salaried earners, by those in receipt of fixed amounts, all of which are ascertainable and capable of computation, and they have all been disallowed through the years, just as they have been disallowed in the case of members of parliament. They have been disallowed on this ground, I think, that if I take a job in Montreal, and I continue to live in Ottawa, and have to travel from Ottawa to Montreal and have my expenses in Montreal, I must have taken that into account when I took the job, and the salary of the job is presumed to be sufficiently attractive to cover those additional expenses, which are not allowed as a deduction from salary.
It is an entirely different matter if I am engaged in a trade or business. It may be argued that "trade or business" includes profession or salaried occupation; but here again the income tax division have been thoroughly consistent and uniform throughout in ruling that "trade or business" does not include salaried positions; they regard that as meaning trade or business in a different sense. The line is very fine, but they have tried to draw it between what they called trade or business on the one hand, and salary which is not a trade or business on the other. Most unfortunately it seems to run through the railway employees, and that is the reason for the difficulty which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned this evening, and which involves us in this situation, that persons on a mileage basis are regarded as not in receipt of wages, salary or other fixed amount; yet persons on a monthly basis are regarded as persons in receipt of wages, salaries or other fixed amount; and therefore a deduction is allowed under section 5, subsection 3, in the one case and is not allowed in the other case. I mention that to show how difficult it is to draw a line between those in the class of trade

or business where the profit, gain or gratuity is not ascertained and capable of computation, on the one side of the line, and those on the other side of the line where that profit, gain or gratuity is ascertained.
That, as I say, has been the practice through the years. As to members of parliament, I am dealing with the matter just as it is, factually, and not expressing any views as to what ought to be done, and whether the law should be changed. But this is the fact, that all of us who have run elections-I have run them since 1926-have done so on the basis that the income tax division was applying that rule of taxation to the sessional indemnity. I knew at the time I accepted nomination in 1926, again in 1930, again in 1935, again in 1940, that I would get $4,000; perhaps for a few years in the thirties we got less. I knew that I was not entitled to any deduction because of my expenses. The fact that I elected to keep up two establishments, one in Nova Scotia and another one here, was the 'basis on which I took the position; it was the basis on which I was elected; it was the basis on which I was taxed before the war and through the war, and there has been no change whatever in the basis of taxation.
The question now arises, should that rule be changed? If it is to be changed there are two ways in which this could be done. We could make a special case for representatives of the public; and I do not think we can confine it to elected representatives of the public, I think it would have to apply to members of the senate and, of course, to members of upper chambers. There is an upper chamber in one of the provinces. I think it would certainly have to apply to members of the lower chambers in the various provinces. Also we have had complaints from municipal councils whose members have to be away part of the time to attend municipal council meetings; they have claimed some deduction as well. I do not think we could apply it to this house alone. Nobody this afternoon had his mind on any body of persons but the body of persons within these four walls.
They did not mention it, but we all recognized it.

I said, I think, that speaking for myself I would shrink from taking a step which would mean a fairly far-reaching change in the prin-

ciples of the taxation system as laid down in that section and adhered to all through the years. Certainly it is a matter to which very careful attention would have to be given, because there is no essential injustice that I can see in the principles of the system as they exist. It may be that a special case can be made. It may be on the ground that the getting of young men into public life is so important, or because the indemnity is not very generous compared' with the indemnity in the United States, and because it is not an attractive career financially-it may be that for reasons like that we ought to apply a rule here which we do not apply outside throughout the length and breadth of the country. But through this war I have thought that we should be terribly careful before we did things like that.
Since the fall of 1941 we 'have had in effect a ceiling policy with regard to wages, salaries and prices. It has been a bitter fight to try to hold those controls. We are told, when we warn about the dangers of inflation and great and vast price rises, that these can be controlled: "It is evident that they can be controlled, because you controlled them". It has been a most unpleasant and disagreeable task trying to control these things, and we have made all kinds of enemies in doing so; but the fact is that those who were in receipt of certain salaries in the fall of 1941 are for the most part in receipt of the same salaries, and yet we have moved in on them with higher and higher taxes until they are caught between the salary ceiling on one side and high taxes on the other. The general principle of war finance in that respect has been that those upon whom high taxes have been placed should really bear high taxes. They should not be enabled in some way or another to get higher remuneration of one kind or another in such a way as to leave themselves in just as good a position as before, to have their standard of living in the same shape as before. We thought that was necessary, being in the straits we were in so far as the war is concerned. We must be careful that those who are caught in that vise of high taxes and frozen salaries will not say to us, the representatives of the people: "You found an out for yourselves by the simple device of freeing a part of your salary or indemnity from taxation." I should not call it salary, because it is not a salary, but it is treated in the act, so far as I can see, just as if it were.
If we treated it as a salary we would be allowed cost of living expense out of it.

The dilemma in which the government seems to find itself may be resolved, if I can put before the committee the following, which I shall attempt at least, by way of two propositions. First of all, the effect of increased taxation since the war where the expense allowance is not incurred, or is not an actual expense. That is the first proposition I wish to illustrate to the committee. Second, where the expense is incurred, but where there is no deduction in arriving at the net taxable income, after allowance for expenses.
The first refers to the motorcar allowance of the ministers, and the second refers to the predicament in which hon. members find themselves. The ministers receive $2,000 as a statutory motorcar allowance. As to the justice or injustice of that, I shall not say anything at the present time, except that probably some ministers cannot spend that $2,000 to-day. They cannot replace their cars, and cannot use very much gasoline.
The ministers can; they have a high rating.

If they are patriotic-and I would assume they are-they cannot. Most of the ministers cannot possibly spend $2,000. This $2,000 is not $2,000 any more; it is now $6,000. The ministers get their ordinary indemnity of $4,000, and a salary of $10,000, making $14,000. If a man in that bracket wishes to get $2,000 extra which he can spend, he has to get an additional $6,000, or a total of $20,000, in order to have $2,000 extra above the $14,000.
Therefore that $2,000 has become magnified into $6,000, because of war taxation. Now, then, what is the obverse of that, namely, the condition in which members find themselves? It is simply this, that members get along on the $4,000 indemnity prior to the war, even with, let us say $1,500 expenses. It might be said to be $2,000 of legitimate expense, which had nothing to do with the cost of elections. Those were simply out-of-pocket expenses in connection with being in Ottawa and earning an indemnity. We will say it was $1,500. But we now find that the tax on this $1,500, which $1,500 we do not retain, has risen from year to year, so that the tax is $750 on something we do not get.
Therefore we may say that whereas we received $4,000 in years prior to the war, on which we paid a negligible tax, and which was available for members with which to keep themselves both here and in their constituencies, they now find that they have $1,500 of expenses, and on that expense, being bracketed between $2,500 and $4,000, there is a tax of approximately fifty per cent, or $750.
So that the ordinary member who is relying on his indemnity has $4,000 gross, and $1,500 as expenses, reducing it to $2,500. And on that $1,500 expense is a further tax of $750. He has about $1,750 left to keep himself. So that you have a position where the minister getting $2,000 more as an allowance, is to-day getting the equivalent of $6,000, whereas the

member who was paying out a certain amount of money, for which he got no allowance or reduction at all, finds that the taxation on that expenditure has gone up from nothing to $750, and his situation in those circumstances has been rendered more difficult.
The parliamentary assistant said that he knew he was going to get $4,000 when he was nominated to come here in 1940. That applies to all of us. It was possible at that time, probably, for us to live on that amount. But to-day it is impossible, with the incidence of heavy taxation, to live on what is left. So that no poor man can possibly live on what is left, and members of the house are in the position in which no other worker, whether he be a wage-earner or a salaried man finds himself to-day. If the minister has any information to the contrary, I should like to have it.
This is a situation which cries out for some alleviation-I might almost say cries out for mercy. But, whether or not anything is done for us this year makes very little difference. -and unsolicited, may I say to the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario. I find myself serving, after taxation, at a net loss, each year. I believe the change came about in this fashion, that the Winnipeg office allowed a deduction in those earlier years, but that more recently, either last year or this year, the allowance made in Winnipeg was rejected by the head office at Ottawa. In any event it appears, if my information is correct, that there was a change made in the application of rales, so far as Canadian National sleeping-car conductors are concerned.
I said earlier that I had a double motive in asking my question. On the one hand I am interested in the subject which has been before the committee this evening, and I am asking whether, if a change has been made in one case, why it cannot be made in another. I am also anxious to know if that change was made, and, if so, why it had to be made to the detriment of this particular group to which I have referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Mr. FRASER, (Northumberland):	I do
not wish to prolong the debate in connection with sessional indemnities, but I should like to make one or two observations. Apparently this afternoon I made the statement that the minister lacked courage, and I want to say that that was in reference only to this particular question. A woman may be very much afraid of a mouse but still have the courage to face death.

Or her

I have no intention of making any reflection upon his courage, except as I said a minute ago.
It is galling to members of parliament when they see these controllers and government
Income War Tax
officials who are appointed not by the civil service commission but by orders in council, ex-bank managers, ex-brokers, chaps who havq been square pegs in round holes, many of them receiving far more than members of parliament and working only five days a week and about six hours a day. They are travelling to and fro all the time cluttering up our trains. As was mentioned by an hon. member across the floor to-night, they receive living allowances that are not taxed. I do not think we should blind ourselves to that fact.
Some of us who have spent a part of our lives doing what we thought was the proper thing in connection with public service should not be blamed for prolonging this debate this afternoon and evening in order to place before the public the exact financial position of members of parliament. I think I can say without fear of contradiction that not one voter in a hundred realizes that a member of parliament pays his own living expenses in Ottawa, and, in many cases, maintains two homes.
The minister has stated that to do what is suggested would constitute a change in the application of taxation during the war, but the hon. member for Rosedale pointed out that wyar-time taxation has changed the whole picture. It has shoved many members into different brackets, and it leaves many members with very .ittle wTith which to maintain their homes or with which to pay their expenses in Ottawa. I think the members have a justifiable case, and I suggest to the minister that he scrutinize carefully the whole matter. As I said a minute ago, there are many officials of the wartime prices and trade board who are running around the country like Greyhound buses and who are allowed living expenses exempt from taxation.
I rose simply to make those two observations, the one in connection with the Minister of Finance and the other to point out that we have a justifiable case. I do not think there will be any change, because I believe the minister has made up his mind, but we have served a purpose by informing the people across Canada that members of parliament are at least not overpaid. Why should "credits for savings" be in there if there is to be no refundable portion? What are you going to take out?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It is really a technical explanation. Section 7A provides for the deduction from the aggregate tax of payments into any superannuation, retirement or pension fund, premiums on life insurance policies and so on. The section makes no difference, so far as the deduction is concerned, between the pure tax and the compulsory savings. In fact, the whole tax is classified as tax. So that if you are taking out a portion of the tax which represents the refundable portion, which is half the tax in the case of the smaller taxpayers and a maximum of ten per cent in the case of the higher taxpayers, you must at the same time deduct the insurance premiums, superannuation and mortgage payments which the taxpayer would otherwise be entitled to deduct as well from his tax. It may be that in revising the section of the law for 1945, another section may be drafted, eliminating this reference to deductions on account of particular savings. It is purely a technical matter. In allowing the removal from the total tax of the savings portion you have also to eliminate the provision for taking members of the house this session. What I credit for the voluntary savings such as life

insurance premiums and mortgage payments made by the taxpayer.
It is misleading to the taxpayer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I agree. It misled me when I read it first and I had to ask for an explanation from the officials. The resolution is misleading, but my hon. friend will find that it will be made clear when the legislation comes down.

The resolution reads, in the first part:
That for 1944 the .total tax on individuals be reduced by one-half the amount of the refundable portion thereof, less one-half credits for savings.
Do these savings have to come in the first half of- the year, or can they be spread over the whole year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They are spread over the whole year. The tax period is the twelve months period. The savings, therefore, are the savings which are made during the tax period. In other words, if your mortgage payment happens to fall due on November 1, it would still be available but only to the extent of one-half in the year 1944.

A different impression was left on my mind by the minister's budget speech. I am glad to have that point cleared up, because I had the impression that the thing automatically stopped on the first day of July and that you could only offset against that, accruals in the form of mortgage payments, life insurance premiums and so on that occurred in the interim. But the parliamentary assistant has made that quite clear. I think that is a concession.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think the misunderstanding arose because it is the withholdings which are cut from the first day of July.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are the cases which I put. There are many cases where persons at least have argued that they have to incur expenses in order to earn the salary that they are paid.
Are they as clear as our case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would think just as clear, yes.
What are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Their case is not quite as clear as some members think, because these expenses that are incurred are living expenses, and living expenses ordinarily are not regarded as expenses in earning an income. I am not making any statement to-night as to what the law is. I am simply going on what the uniform interpretation has been by the income tax division. Even they may have been wrong; I do not know. I think opinions have been given by lawyers that the expenses could be deducted because members of parliament were similar to a trade or business, or for some other reason. But even if that hurdle were taken, the question remains whether hotel expenses and restaurant expenses and room expenses that a person incurs are expenses
incurred in earning the indemnity. I suppose that, strictly speaking, a member could change his place of residence during the time of the session if he wished to do so.

That
would not help him at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question with respect to this item. The minister has indicated' that the withdrawal of the compulsory savings feature will result in an annual loss of revenue to the government of about $110,000,000. That would seem to indicate that there has been some figuring done about this, and I am wondering if the minister can give any break-down of that $110,000,000 among the various income brackets.
The reason why I ask that question is this. The minister and the Minister of Justice, in opposing the idea of raising the inoome tax exemption levels, pointed out, and I say quite rightly, that unless you make adjustments in the tax rates it would mean a greater saving to those in the upper income brackets than to those for whose benefit the proposal was made. The point we tried to make was that if you raise the income tax exemption levels you would have to adjust the rates in the upper brackets, and we asked that that be done. The minister has made it clear that it was not his policy to give greater relief to those in the upper brackets than to those in the lower brackets, and I am wondering if he can tell us how the two classes would be affected here. Is it not the case-or has he figures to refute what I am saying?-that the greater part of this $110,000,000 of relief will go to those in the upper income brackets?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be very hard to make an estimate as between income groups. Everyone who is acquainted with the matter believes that it is the taxpayers in the highest income groups who have the offsets.
That is what I tried to suggest.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That may be. That is the reason why I was asking whether the minister had the figures or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it is true that after you hit a certain medium income taxpayer, for the most part the people above that are not having any compulsory savings deducted, because it is covered by insurance premiums and payments of that kind. Therefore the cash benefit of removing the compulsory savings is, we think, largely in the low income groups.

After all, it is just a guess on the part of the department and the minister. There is no calculation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

When you get down to sisters-in-law, sons-in-law and dlaughters-in-law I think you are going the limit. I am willing that the older people should be taken care of, that an allowance should be granted to the taxpayer for his mother-in-law or his father-in-law or his grandparents-in-law, but I think the minister owes us some explanation for having taken in sons-in-law. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Before you leave the item it seeems to me that 'this is the only resolution among the number before us on which I can ask a question which was raised by at least three hon. members during the debate on the budget motion; I refer to the question of an allowance to parents of student nurses under the reference just quoted by the hon. member for Peterborough West with regard to educational institutions. It is a matter about which I wrote some time ago to the Minister of National Revenue and also to the Minister of Finance, and as I say, other hon. members joined me in speaking about it during the main debate; they are not in the chamber just now, or I am sure they would support me in asking this question. I know the answer that is made, namely, that these student nurses are supposed to receive certain remuneration and certain assistance while they are in training. But the parents of all of them, at least those who have written me, are terribly conscious of the expenses to which they are put in order to assist their daughters in going through for the nursing .profession. I have in mind also the fact that the government considers in its whole taxation policy the things which are desirable, such as full production and the encouragement of people to go in for professions which are needed1. Here is a very important and necessary profession, and parents who have written me in cases like this feel quite discouraged because they are not allowed an exemption for daughters between eighteen and twenty-one attending nursing schools. They claim that this should be granted under the heading of "educational institutions," and I feel they are right. Could the minister make a statement on the matter?

Representations having been made to me by students, I wrote to the department in fulfilment of a promise I made, and I received the answer, if I recall rightly, that it was a question of degree. When students over eighteen years of age go to college the expense is much more substantial-travelling, clothing, board and lodging. Students in a nursing school get board and lodging free, and washing as well, but the allowance is pitiful. At least, that is my experience in a hospital I know something about. While nurses are in training they do not get enough to clothe them.
Some of them do not get anything.

I would be astonished if there were nursing schools now where they do not get anything, because these girls work strenuously and work long hours. I have observed them as a patient in a hospital and I know exactly what the labour is. It is a question of degree of drain on the parents and I quite agree that the situations are different. Nevertheless the principle is the same. Perhaps some limited allowance should be made for this and I should like to know the reaction of the department. I add my voice to that of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre because of the insistence of some of my own constituents who have experienced some difficulty in this matter. There is a great shortage of nurses and we ought to encourage nursing. We are encouraging doctors to go into the army, and we might encourage girls to go into nursing schools on the same theory by which we are helping the doctors. There is some merit in the matter and, as I stated, in my opinion, it is just a matter of degree.

While, as the hon. member for YorkJSunbury says, it is a matter of degree, the girls who go in for nursing are engaged for the whole year, whereas many of the students who go to university are able during the summer vacation to assist in the payment of university fees. The girls who are nursing are employed the full year and they receive a very small amount. If you inquire at the hospitals you will find that it is usually about $10 a month, and out of that there are certain levies that are made by the hospital, which reduces it to about half that amount.
In some cases to nothing.

Yes. If a girl happens to break a thermometer or some other equipment she must pay for it, and quite often the girls find that at the end of the month they have nothing coming to them. The parents have to buy their uniforms when they go in-
